scenario: AITA For telling my Girlfriend she needs to quit whining about who eats what or I'll kick her out | Well, the title says it all, the past few weeks have both been really great and extremely infuriating. We don't live together, but we decided it would be best to stick together during these times as we have no family near as such she is staying with me as I have my own apartment and she has multiple roommates hence the choice. Well she eats more then any person I have ever known, especially considering her physical appearance, she is 5'4, petite, thin and yet she eats more than I do and I am 6'6 and a bit of a gymbro. To put it in to perspective, our food bill each week is roughly three times compared to what I usually spend alone. Yet she seems extremely selfconcious about this and as a result will act surprised when something is gone, try to blame me, states I am eating too much whenever I eat anything, essentially, she tries to deflect her eating habits and projects them on to me out of embarrassment about her eating so much I guess? The thing is, I don't care about her eating habits, she can eat whatever she wants to eat what I am done with is her constantly trying to blame me, whining about food and picking fights about it. I talked to her about it multiple times, argued with her about it multiple times but earlier today I just got so tired of another comment, this time brought on by me making a sandwhich at 2 PM when I had eaten at 10 AM I know right, horrible. So I told her that this crap was either going to stop right here and now or I'll kick her out and she can spend the coming weeks or months at her own place. She just started crying, called me horrible and locked herself in the bathroom. At this point I just dont get it anymore, am I being TA here or is she TA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I need to figure out whether the action described in the scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if it's okay for him to tell his girlfriend she needs to quit whining about food or he'll kick her out. 

First, I'll try to understand the situation. They're not living together, but she's staying with him because she has multiple roommates and he has his own apartment. He's noticing that she eats a lot more than him, even though she's petite and thin. This is causing their food bill to triple compared to when he was alone. He's tried talking to her about it multiple times, but she keeps deflecting and blaming him. He got so frustrated that he told her to stop or he'd kick her out, which made her cry and lock herself in the bathroom.

Now, I need to evaluate if his action is morally acceptable. Morally acceptable actions usually consider respect, fairness, and the well-being of others. So, let's break it down.

He's frustrated because her eating habits are affecting their finances and causing arguments. He's tried to communicate, but she's not changing her behavior. Telling her to stop or else might seem like a way to enforce boundaries, but it's also a threat. Threatening to kick her out when she's staying with him because she has no other family nearby could be seen as unfair, especially if she's in a vulnerable situation.

On the other hand, he's trying to set boundaries to maintain his own peace of mind and financial stability. It's reasonable to expect that guests respect the household's resources. However, the way he's handling it might be harsh. Instead of threatening, maybe a calmer discussion about shared responsibilities or finding a solution together would be better.

Also, considering her reaction—crying and locking herself in the bathroom—it shows that his words had a strong emotional impact. This might indicate that his approach was too confrontational and could be seen as emotionally abusive, even if unintentional.

So, while he has reasons for being frustrated, the method he used to address the issue might not be the most morally acceptable. It could be seen as unfair and hurtful, especially if she's in a difficult situation and relies on him for support.
